title: Mahapajapati's thanks
hookLine: the foster mother's song of thanks to the one she raised (Therigatha, Mahapajapati)

lines: THANKS THAT RUN THE OTHER WAY.
cards: Hero. That's the word she uses, bowing to a man she once fed as a baby. The woman is Mahapajapati Gotami.

She was the sister of the Buddha's mother, Maya, and when Maya died, the texts say, she raised the boy as her own. Much later, she has gone forth herself, and her song is in the collection of the sisters.
A child thanking a parent is a familiar scene. This song runs the other way.

teach.b: First, the opening. Buddha, hero, homage to you, she says, highest of beings, who freed me from suffering, and many other people too. The woman who once held him now bows.
In lives before this one, she says, she has been a mother, a son, a father, a brother, a grandmother, wandering on without seeing how things are.
Parent and child, in her telling, are parts played many times, in both directions.

teach.h: A CLOTH, AND A DEBT BOTH WAYS.
teach.b: Third, a gift that goes both ways. In the Majjhima, a teaching on offerings begins with Mahapajapati bringing the Buddha new cloth she made herself. He asks her to give it to the whole community.
Ananda speaks up for her: she was your mother's sister, your nurse, the one who fed you with her own milk when your mother died.

And, Ananda adds, the help ran the other way too: through the Buddha she found refuge and the teaching. The Buddha agrees, and says a debt like that is not easy to repay. Neither debt cancels the other.
Fourth, the close of the song.
Truly, she says, Maya gave birth to Gotama for the good of many. So she honors her sister too, the mother who didn't live to see any of it.
And honoring the Buddhas, she says, looks like disciples together in harmony, energetic, steady in effort.
Her thanks become a picture of people still practicing.

how: Buddhist communities remember Mahapajapati Gotami as the Buddha's foster mother and as the woman whose request, in the Vinaya, opened ordination to women.

o: Maya's blessing on her newborn son
a foster mother's thanks to the son she raised
a son's thanks to the mother who raised him

games.q: Mahapajapati and the one she raised: tap the pairs.
p: raised the boy as her own
speaks up for her gift of cloth
how the Buddhas are honored, she says

s: Mahapajapati's song thanks the one she raised
she calls the Buddha hero and thanks him for freeing her, and many others.
in her song, she has only ever been a mother
she says that in lives before she was mother, son, father, brother and grandmother.
in the Majjhima story, the debt runs one way only
Ananda says how much she did for him, and adds that she gained much through him too. the Buddha agrees.

games.q: you're Ananda. the Buddha's foster mother has brought him cloth she made herself, and he's asked her to give it to the whole community instead. what do you do?
o: say nothing. it isn't your place.
speak up and remind him what she did for him.
take the cloth to the community yourself.
games.why: Ananda reminds him she was his nurse and fed him when his mother died, and adds that she found refuge through him. the Buddha agrees: the debt runs both ways.

practice: Bring one person to mind: a parent, a grandparent, an aunt, a teacher, an older brother or sister, or a child who is grown now.

Find one specific thing to thank them for, a meal, a ride in the rain, a hard conversation they didn't avoid, and hold it for a few breaths. If they're no longer living, thanks can still be spoken in the heart.

wordCard.voice: Mahapajapati's thanks. The foster mother's song to the one she raised: homage to you, hero, who freed me and many others. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali namo: homage. Mahapajapati's song opens with homage to the Buddha she once raised.

carryVoice: Your line: thanks to the child. Here the gratitude runs both ways at once. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 142 (Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta, the teaching on offerings)
